html:
Mistra, or Mystras, is a ruined medieval town on a steep hill above ancient Sparta, in the Peloponnese of Greece. It began as a castle built in 1249 by the Frankish prince William of Villehardouin of Achaea.

William was captured by the Byzantines at Pelagonia in 1259 and had to hand over Mistra and other forts to win his freedom in 1262. A town grew below the castle and became the capital of the Despotate of the Morea, ruled by princes of the imperial family, often the emperor's sons or brothers.

In the 14th and 15th centuries it was a last centre of Byzantine culture. Churches such as the Peribleptos and the Pantanassa were painted with fine frescoes, and the philosopher Gemistos Plethon taught a revived Platonism there. Constantine XI, the last emperor, was proclaimed at Mistra in 1449. The Ottomans took the town in 1460, seven years after the fall of Constantinople. It was abandoned in the 1830s for the new town of Sparta and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sum: Mistra, or Mystras, is a ruined medieval town on a steep hill above ancient Sparta, in the Peloponnese of Greece. It began as a castle built in 1249 by the Frankish prince William of Villehardouin of Achaea.
